cards.title: Deciding whether SEO is worth pursuing for a Shopify store
cards.summary: A pre-investment filter for judging if organic search can become a profitable channel or a waste of months.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest budget, time or agency fees into SEO for your store, before writing any content.
steps: Ask the core question first: do people already search for what you sell? SEO only captures existing demand, it does not create it. The source (Dave Fogerty) argues that if you invented a genuinely new product nobody searches for, SEO cannot help.
Check Google search volume and commercial intent for your main category terms. If people rarely Google your category, content will not rank or convert.
Test margin math: SEO favours stores with healthy AOV and margins. If AOV is low or margins are razor thin, the content investment may never pay back.
Recognise the source's binary framing: for most Shopify brands SEO is either the most profitable channel or a huge waste of time, with little middle ground.

Treat this as a channel-diversification play, not a replacement: the source's Calming Blankets example kept selling via SEO when Meta ads broke repeatedly, but that is one brand's case, not a guarantee.
If those tests pass, commit to bottom-funnel, conversion-intent keywords rather than general blog traffic, which the source says is close to worthless in 2025.
caveats: Source's 10M first-year revenue and #1 ranking in 6 months are one brand's anecdote, not a benchmark.
The 'SEO is all or nothing' framing is the presenter's opinion, not a measured rule.

cards.title: Capturing branded search your paid ads create
cards.summary: Paid awareness generates branded searches that a competitor may capture if you don't rank for your own name.
cards.use_when: Planning paid acquisition or auditing whether competitors outrank you on your own brand and category terms.
steps: Accept that Meta and other paid ads create latent demand: people see the ad, don't click, then Google your brand or product later. The source calls this branded search.
Check whether your site ranks for your own brand name and the generic product term your ads promote.
If you don't rank, a smaller competitor can appear first and take the sale you paid to generate. The source frames this as one brand funding awareness while another captures conversion.
Protect the conversion path by ensuring a product or collection page (not just homepage) ranks for the branded and category search.
Pair this with the source's keyword-structure hack: build collection pages targeting the variations people Google after seeing an ad.
This is a defensive play on existing spend, not a reason to add SEO budget on top of everything else.
caveats: Source gives no data on how much paid spend leaks to competitors; treat the mechanism as a hypothesis to verify in your own Search Console.
Requires that people actually Google your category, which the source says is not universal.

cards.title: Multiplying collection pages to target keyword variations
cards.summary: Replace one broad collection page with many specific sub-collection pages that reuse the same products.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a product category where you currently have a single broad collection page competing on one high-difficulty term.
steps: Take your bestselling category and list the different ways people search for it: e.g., hoodies splits into men's hoodies, oversized hoodies, zip hoodies, running hoodies, hoodies under $50.
Build a separate collection (or landing) page for each variation. You can include the same products; you're changing presentation, not inventory.
Validate each keyword in Ahrefs or Semrush: set the keyword difficulty filter below 35 and look for commercial intent (check the current interface, these tools change).
Sanity-check by Googling the keyword: if other collection pages rank, you likely can too. If only giants like Nike rank, it's probably too competitive.
Respect one keyword per page and never target the same keyword with both a product page and a collection page. The source calls this keyword cannibalization and says it will tank results.
This converts one unwinnable competitive term into many smaller, easier terms that accumulate traffic.
caveats: Keyword difficulty guidance (<35) is a source-specific heuristic, not a universal threshold.
Requires genuine search variation; splitting a category into terms nobody searches adds no value.

cards.title: The four blog formats that still drive ecommerce revenue
cards.summary: Replace lifestyle and seasonal blog content with four bottom- and mid-funnel formats built for buyer intent.
cards.use_when: Planning a content calendar or auditing existing blog posts that get traffic but no sales.
steps: Stop producing the formats the source calls dead in ecommerce: seasonal lifestyle posts, generic listicles, trend pieces, and tips that apply to everyone and sell to no one.

Format 1 - You vs competitors: target 'brand A vs brand B' searches by decision-stage buyers. Mentioning a competitor's name can help you rank for their branded search and introduce yourself as the stronger option.
Format 2 - Alternatives to competitors: target 'alternatives to X' and 'best X alternatives' searches, list options and position yourself first to convert people outside your funnel.
Format 3 - Best [product type] for [use case]: target clear buying intent like 'best eye serums for women over 50'; match product to need and target low-difficulty longtail terms.
Format 4 - Buying guides: long-form evergreen content that educates hesitant buyers and naturally earns backlinks that lift domain authority.
Before writing any post, check the SERP: if blogs rank, write the blog; if it's all collection pages, build that page instead.

The source claims 10-15 well-targeted posts can build this system, and cites a client (Simbotanica) ranking #3 for a competitor's brand name within a week of implementing two competitor-focused formats.
caveats: The Simbotanica ranking-in-a-week result is an anecdote, not a benchmark.
Only works for products with existing search demand.

cards.title: Building an internal linking system that funnels authority to money pages
cards.summary: Use controlled internal links to push SEO value and user flow toward collection and product pages that convert.
cards.use_when: Optimising an existing store with orphaned blog posts and product pages that never get internal links.
steps: Identify your money pages: the collection and product pages where conversion happens.
Write top- and mid-funnel blogs with the linking flow decided upfront, not bolted on later.
Link from each blog to a money page within the first 100-200 words, then add three to five internal links to related blogs later in the article.
Use descriptive anchor text of two to four words that matches the product. Avoid 'click here' and avoid using your brand name as anchor text.
Link collections from general to specific: e.g., from a collagen supplements collection down to a hair loss collagen for women sub-collection.
Start with your top two to three highest-traffic blog posts and add a clean relevant link from each to your bestselling collection or product page.
Repeat until the site is a connected web. The source claims each link takes seconds and can meaningfully shift monthly revenue.
caveats: Internal links transfer value but cannot fix a site with no external authority or no existing traffic.
The $100 vs $1,000 per month difference is a source claim, not a measured outcome.

cards.title: Getting cited in AI search results (GEO)
cards.summary: Structure product and content pages with high specificity so AI tools quote your store in generated answers.
cards.use_when: Adapting your PDPs, collections and content for AI Overviews, Perplexity or ChatGPT-style answers that bypass the ten blue links.
steps: Accept the shift the source calls GEO: AI tools summarise multiple sources into one answer, so if you're not cited you may as well not exist for that query.
Note the source's cited study of 768,000+ AI citations: over half came from product pages, comparison content and buying guides, not news or homepages.
Split broad collections into specific use-case pages (e.g., mineral sunscreen for sensitive skin, mineral sunscreen for dry skin) reusing the same products but matching exact query language.
Refresh comparison blogs ('brand A vs brand B', 'best collagen supplements for women over 40') so AI tools have citable, question-shaped content.
Test by Googling your product type phrased as a question, e.g., 'What hoodie is best for me?', and study which pages get cited in any AI overview.
Audit each collection: can it be split into individual needs or situations? The source says need-specific pages tend to outperform in both AI and organic search.
Make cited pages skimable, useful and product-focused so both AI tools and humans can extract an answer.
caveats: The 768,000-citation study is reported second-hand; treat the exact split as indicative, not verified.
GEO is an emerging channel with uncertain durability; the source frames it as early-mover arbitrage.

input.source_name: Steal These Shopify SEO Hacks To Rank #1 Overnight.docx
input.text: You can rank number one on Google and still make absolutely nothing if you hit the right search term. It can print money every single month. Within 6 months, we ranked number one. The brand did 10 million of revenue in its first year. In a world of AI generated answers, only the best content is going to be seen. Most people think ranking number one on Google takes years, but for e-commerce, that's just not true anymore. With the right setup, you can start driving high converting organic traffic without relying on other paid ads or expensive agencies. My name is Dave Fogerty and I've built the Udy, a wearable blanket brand into 800 million in sales and I've helped over a,000 7 figure founders through my program Daily Mentor. In this video, I'm going to show you four advanced SEO hacks designed for Shopify brands. How to know if your SEO is worth your time, how to rank for more terms with the same product, and how to get your brand showing up in AI search results. If done right, SEO can become your most profitable, consistent channel. Let's get into it. But first, should you even care about SEO? Most people think SEO is just something you should just be doing, like it's a box to tick. But the reality is for most Shopify brands, SEO is either your most profitable sales channel or a massive waste of time. There's just no in between. You can rank number one on Google, get thousands of views to your site, and still make absolutely nothing because you've ranked for the wrong thing. And yet, if you hit the right search term in the right category at the right times, it can print money every single month without paying a scent on ads. Back when I launched my first brand, Calming Blankets, I was spending big on Facebook. That was our main growth engine. But I noticed something. Weighted blankets, the term, was getting searched a ton on Google. So, I started optimizing our site for SEO. Within 6 months, we ranked number one. The brand did 10 million of revenue in its first year. Even when Facebook ads broke, which it did multiple times, our SEO kept running and it kept driving sales. But here's the part no one tells you. SEO isn't always a good idea. If you've invented something brand new like a product, nobody's ever searched for SEO is just not going to help. There's no demand to capture. Also, if your AOV is too low, if your margins are razor thin, or if people just don't Google your category very often, you waste months writing content that never ranks and never converts. And that's exactly what I think most brands do. They think SEO is either something that's just broken on their site or just another task sitting on their to-do list. So they hire an agency, write a 100 blogs, and wait months for magic to happen. But it never does. In 2025, blog traffic and rankings alone are almost worthless. What matters is intent. Bottomfunnel keywords, conversion. SEO isn't all about traffic. It's about catching and converting people who are already searching to buy. And when it's done right, it's one of the most profitable channels you'll ever touch. This happens a lot in eop. You spend big on meta ads. more people see your brand and that visibility drives branded search. People see your ad, don't click, and just Google your product later. But what if your site doesn't rank? Guess what? A smaller competitor does. One brand spends thousands driving awareness through paid ads, while another ranks ahead of them in search and captures all of those sales. They didn't run ads. They didn't outspend anyone. They just showed up first on Google, and that was enough to win the customer. So before we get into the hacks, ask yourself, do people already want what you're selling? If the answer is yes, then the next part is where things get really, really exciting. So hack one, advanced keyword optimization. Most stores have one collection page per product type. One for hoodies, one for t-shirts, one for sneakers. That makes sense at first glance, but it's also one of the biggest missed opportunities in ecom SEO because what you're really doing is betting everything on a single keyword such as hoodies, t-shirts, or sneakers. Those terms are ultra competitive, hard to rank for, and very, very broad. But here's the thing, the same product can be searched a dozen different ways, and each variation opens up a new opportunity to rank. So instead of trying to win one page for hoodies, you could add five or 10 separate different pages targeting men's hoodies, oversized hoodies, zip hoodies, running hoodies, hoodies under $50. And in most cases, those pages could include some of the exact same products. They're the same pages, just targeting something different. You're changing nothing about your inventory. You're just changing how it's presented to match how people actually search. And the result is that you go from fighting over one massively competitive keyword to only dozens of smaller, easier ones. And it just adds up fast. Now, you might be thinking this is about tricking Google, but it's just not. It's about aligning with search intent. Someone searching for a twoperson hot tub has a very different search intent than someone searching commercial hot tub or luxury spa bar. Even if the product is technically the same, most brands ignore this. But the ones who are winning with SEO in 2025 are doing the complete opposite. They're building out subolctions that target every variation of demand and ranking faster with less effort. So, how do you apply this to your store? Start with your bestselling product category. Let's say it's just skinincare. Ask yourself, what are the variations people might be searching for such as anti-aging face serum, vegan face serum, facial creams under $30? Each of these can become its own category. Each can rank independently and each can capture a different kind of customer. You can use and find these keywords by using tools like ah refs or sem rush. Go into one of these tools, set the difficulty filter below 35. Look for commercial intent. They all of these tools have this. And when in doubt, just Google the keyword. If you see other collection pages ranking, it means you can too. If you see Nike ranking for them and it's extremely competitive, maybe you can't. One important rule though is only target one keyword per page. Never try to rank both a product page and a collection page for the same keyword. That's called keyword cannibalization and it will tank your results. But done right, this is one of the fastest ways to multiply your visibility. No extra ads, no extra content, no extra products, just smarter structure and smarter results. That hack that I just described is huge. But what if you could generate traffic, rank faster, and convert higher all without touching your product pages? And this brings us to hack number two, which is the only e-commerce blogs that still work. Cuz blog content is basically dead in e-commerce. Most of it doesn't rank, it doesn't drive traffic, and it sure as hell doesn't drive revenue. That's because most brands are still stuck writing blogs like it's 2014. They chase seasonal topics. They write lifestyle fluff. They publish generic advice that applies to everyone and sells to no one. You've seen the usual ones such as how to stay cozy in winter, five fun facts about skincare, top fashion trends this year. The problem is none of these actually match how people shop. They might get a few clicks, but they won't rank long-term and they won't bring in buyers. Worse, they waste time and dilute what's called your site's authority. The brands that are winning in SEO in 25 are doing something completely different. They're using four specific blog formats, not for clicks, not for brand awareness, but to rank in the terms that actually bring in buyers. These blog formats target bottom and middlefunnel search terms. They rank fast, they convert, and they attract back links from other publications, including directories and even Google AI generated answers. So, let me break them all down for you. You've got you verse competitors. These posts target people searching things like brand A versus brand B. They're weighing their options and actively looking to make a decision. But here's the trick. Just mentioning the competitor's name can help you rank for their branded search. That means you can show up when someone searches their name and introduce yourself as the stronger option. Even if that customer wasn't considering you before, they now are. Two, alternatives to competitors. So that will be your blog name. Same principle, different angle. These posts catch people looking to move away from a competitor such as best flasks alternatives to Hydro Flask or best alternatives to the hoodie. Don't do that. That's a high intense search. You list the options and put yourself first. It reframes your product as the smarter choice, more modern choice and gives you a shot at converting customers who were never in your funnel to begin with. Then third, we got best product type four use case. This is where people are searching with clear buying intent such as best eye serums for women over 50. They've already decided to buy. They're just looking for the right fit. If your product generally matches what they need and your content feels trustworthy, you win. This format also gives you a way to target dozens of longtail keywords with lower competition and faster ranking times. But remember, before you write, always check the SER. If blogs are ranking, go for it. If it's all collection pages, skip the blog and build that instead. Then fourth, we've got buying guides, which is long- form evergreen pieces of content that educate and convert, such as the complete buying guide to a sauna or how to choose the right skinincare routine. These are great for buyers who are curious but hesitant. A good guide makes them feel informed, confident, and ready to make the purchase. These also naturally earn back links over time which can boost your overall domain authority and help other pages rank faster. So together these four blog types create a simple but powerful system. They rank for commercial intent keywords. They capture ready to buy traffic. They support your product and collection pages. And becoming more important, they rank highly in AI searches and you don't need dozens of posts. You can build this system with 10 to 15 well targeted blocks. Kai Cromwell, our SEO coach at Daily Mentor, helped one of our clients, Simbotanica, implement two of these competitor focused blog formats. And less than a week later, they were ranking number three on Google for their main competitor's brand name. So, how do we apply this? Start by looking at all of the people who are already searching around your competitors. If these are high volume searches like competitor A versus competitor B or alternatives to competitor A, you can use that traffic to drive your advantage. Write your own versions of the comparison. Include your brand. Make a case for it, a truthful case for it. Even if you're not being searched yet, you can still show up as a result next to brands that are. That's how you piggy back off demand that already exists instead of trying to generate your own from scratch. This is how e-commerce blogs actually move the needle in 2025. Smart content that captures demand, builds authority, and drives real sales. However, even the best blogs just won't work if nobody sees them. If you want them to rank, support your product pages and actually drive sales. They need to be connected. So, this brings us to hack number three, internal linking. Internal linking is one of the most overlooked SEO levers in e-commerce. Most store owners don't even know about it or they just massively underestimate the impact. But done right, it can instantly rank your site. We're not talking about backlinks here. We're talking about something that you fully control. how your own pages connect between each other. Internal links help Google crawl your site faster. They distribute SEO value to your most important pages and they tell Google which pages matter the most so they rank higher. So, here's what poor internal linking usually looks like. Random blog posts with no structure, product pages that never get linked to, and a few scattered links in your footer or header and that's it. But the brands that are winning at SEO have an actual system. It starts with content. Top ofunnel and middle of funnel blogs are written with the intent of linking into your core collection pages. Those collection pages are what we call money pages. And this is where the conversion happens. Every blog should be written with this flow in mind. Link to your money pages in the first 100 to 200 words. Add three to five internal links to related blogs later in the article. This does two things. First, it pushes the authority to the key pages so they rank higher. And secondly, it keeps people on your site longer, moving them towards the purchase. And it doesn't stop at blogs either. You should build links between collections from general to specific. For example, if someone lands on your collagen supplements collection page, link to a subolction like hair loss collagen for women. You're not just helping Google understand your structure. You're nudging users closer to the exact thing that they actually want. And this stuff compounds because most backlinks point to your homepage or blog post, not your product pages. Internal links are what transfer the value where it counts. So, how do we apply this? First, you want to pick your top two to three highest traffic blog posts. Add a clean, relevant link from each of them to your bestselling collection or product page. Then use anchor text that clearly describes what the user is clicking to. Not click here, not your brand name, just two to four words that match the product. Then go to the same collection page and link down into your more specific subolctions. Repeat this until your entire site is like a connected spiderweb. That's how you build internal authority. That's how you help pages rank faster. And the best part is this is all free. takes 10 seconds per link and can make the difference between $100 a month or $1,000 a month. But even if your internal linking is perfect, there's one big shift happening in search that most brands still aren't ready for and it's already changing what shows up on Google. So this brings us to hack number four. Get ahead of generative search or also known as geo. Gio is how to get your brand cited inside AI powered search tools like GPT perlexity, Google's new AI overviews, all of that kind of stuff. This is the future of search and it's already happening. Instead of 10 blue links, users are getting answers directly from Google. AI tools pull from multiple sources and summarize them into single blocks. That means that if you're not in that summary, you may as well not exist. We looked at a study with over 768,000 AI citations. More than half of all the content that the AI tools cited came from product pages, comparisonstyle content, and buying guides, not blogs that a lot of people are doing, not news articles, and definitely not your homepage. So, how do we show up? The key is specificity. AI tools want to site content that directly answers a specific user's question. So instead of one sunscreen's collection, you split it out into multiple as I've talked about like mineral sunscreen for sensitive skin or mineral sunscreen for dry skin. Each one can include the same core products, but the structure and language to match exactly the specificity what users are searching for because this does two things. It increases your odds of showing up in that generative search result. It also boosts your ranking across more longtail keywords. This also applies to blogs, the kind that I mentioned in hack number two. If you write comparison blogs like brand A versus brand B, top seven competitors to competitor, or best collagen supplements for women over 40, you give AI tools the kind of content that they love to site. You're not writing to just get clicks from search results. You're writing to be quoted directly inside AI generated answers. So, how do you apply this? Start by googling your main product type, but phrase it like a question. See what kind of results come from Google. For example, something like, "What hoodie is best for me?" If an AI overview comes up, study what pages are being cited for that answer. Next, look at your collections. Ask yourself, could this collection be split into more specific use cases because pages built around individual needs or situations tend to outperform best in both geo and organic search terms.
